claim: Johnson and Blair (1977, 1994/2006) and Govier define a good argument by three tests: acceptable, relevant and sufficient premises. Later NLP work operationalises exactly these and nests them locally (cogency) and globally (reasonableness).
agent_test: Give the Verify step the ARS checklist for open answers vs a free-form 'check your answer' prompt, equal tokens, blind judge.

claim: Humans agree well that a premise set is insufficient in essays overall (alpha .77, 91.07% on 433 arguments) but agreement collapses on contested cases: alpha .14 on the 32% of items where any annotator flagged insufficiency. Headline agreement overstates reliability.
agent_test: Report agreement of our judge only on hard items; do not trust overall agreement.

claim: Relevance and acceptability are harder for humans to agree on than sufficiency in essays: kappa .435 (relevance) and .259 (acceptability) in the error analysis.
agent_test: Acceptability verdicts need an external source or explicit uncertainty marking; test whether the agent flags unsupported-but-plausible premises.

claim: In real debate arguments, expert agreement on ARS dimensions is only moderate (alpha at most .22 for seven annotators), and sufficiency is the weakest or least stable dimension across humans, crowd and LLMs.
agent_test: Treat sufficiency verdicts as noisy; take a majority over several samples rather than one verdict.

claim: Real arguments are mostly weak on sufficiency (172 of 304 low local; 231 of 304 low global) and mostly relevant (124 high, 155 medium of 304). Lack of enough support, not irrelevance, is the common defect; LLM answers show the same pattern (relevance failure under 0.5%).
agent_test: Spend the checklist effort on sufficiency (what is missing, counter-arguments), not relevance.

claim: Premises alone predict sufficiency: a classifier on premises matches the full-input model (F1 .875 vs .885); a generated conclusion adds nothing (.532 alone).
agent_test: Compare premises-only sufficiency judgement vs with-conclusion; expect no gain from re-deriving the conclusion.

claim: Weak-support cues are lexical (examples, personal experience); a CNN reaches .843 accuracy (92.5% of human .911), and length is a strong confound in quality labels.
agent_test: Test the judge on length-matched pairs and anecdote-heavy answers.

claim: Crowd workers rate ARS dimensions reliably only when at least 10 ratings are pooled; crowd-vs-expert alpha on mean ratings: acceptability .49, relevance .42, local sufficiency .18, cogency .27.
agent_test: Pool several independent judge samples for sufficiency; one rating is noisy.

claim: LLM judges are far more self-consistent than humans (alpha .6 to .98 vs about .37-.40) but consistency is not validity: agreement with humans is moderate and weakest for sufficiency.
agent_test: Do not read judge self-agreement as accuracy; validate against a gold set.

claim: Judge configuration moves LLM-human agreement a lot: GPT-4o listwise with self-consistency reaches alpha .47 cogency, .57 local sufficiency, .53 global sufficiency; GPT-3.5 pointwise ranges -.40 to .64; dimension order changes alpha (e.g. .203 vs .447); zero-shot beat few-shot; averaging three orders costs two extra calls.
agent_test: At equal tokens compare one pointwise check vs listwise with 3 samples.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-10 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Adding LLM annotations to human panels raises agreement for PaLM 2 (expert .40 to .50 with 5) but lowers it for GPT-3/3.5. The effect is model-specific.
agent_test: Only relevant if a human-labelled panel is built for our judge.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-10 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Pairwise judging by open LLMs of logic quality is only moderate: best Llama-70B few-shot Pearson .474, kappa .493, 53.0% agreement vs majority baseline kappa .442 (48.3%). Chain-of-thought often lowered agreement; few-shot helped only large models.
agent_test: Do not assume CoT improves verification; compare with and without at equal tokens.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-10 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Very small judges fail: models under about 7B are near random on debate speeches; large judges match or exceed single-human agreement but score lower than humans.
agent_test: Use the strong model for the Verify judge.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-10 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Supplying LLM-generated context (assumptions, counter-argument, feedback) to a scorer improves cogency prediction: Spearman .348 to .424 (BERT dual encoder).
agent_test: Test generating a counter-argument before judging sufficiency.

claim: A counterfactual-objection check for sufficiency (CASA) beats plain prompting: macro-F1 73.4 vs 66.8 zero-shot (BIG-bench fallacy set, Llama-2-7B); objections judged more rational (92% vs 90%) and revisions better 58% vs 7% worse. Only small open models tested; ablating the intervention drops macro-F1 to 65.8.
agent_test: Prompt 'imagine a case where the premises hold but the conclusion fails'; compare with generic verify at equal tokens.

claim: Frontier models defending moral verdicts almost never fail relevance (<0.5%) but fail grounds and sufficiency: 18.2% of judge cells, 67.8% of failures from two models; judge pair agreed 89.6%. Low-grounds answers are not longer; they hedge more.
agent_test: Run ARS scoring on our agent's open answers to find where it fails.

claim: Models defend their reasoning trace better than their post-hoc justification on Govier dimensions (positive local advantage in all 8 models).
agent_test: Check whether the final justification is verified against the trace.

claim: LLM debaters are persuaded more often by fallacious than by logical arguments (GPT-3.5 17% vs 10%; GPT-4 56% vs 37%); the stronger model is more susceptible. The stated '41% and 69% more likely' does not follow from those raw figures.
agent_test: Adversarial test: feed fallacious support to the Verify step and measure acceptance.

claim: GPT-4 detects named fallacies at 0.79 accuracy (3-shot, N=780); the 0.90 figure excludes 'None' outputs; Appeal to Emotion often missed.
agent_test: Fallacy naming is not a substitute for ARS evaluation.

claim: LLM-generated Walton critical questions (probes for acceptability, relevance, sufficiency of a scheme) are useful at most about 57% of the time zero-shot; annotator agreement .54.
agent_test: Test critical-question generation as the Verify move vs free critique.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-10 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Laypeople discriminate strong from weak arguments much like experts (strong minus weak 1.30 vs 1.61 points; r=.62 with expert panel, N=278), moderated by analytic thinking (r about .30) and slightly hurt by overconfidence (-.15).
agent_test: Baseline: unaided judgement already separates gross cases; gains lie in subtle cases.

claim: Argument strength is graded and content-dependent (Bayesian view), a rival to a form-only checklist: the same form can be strong or weak depending on priors and source reliability. No study compares a checklist with probability-based strength ratings for LLMs; verbalised LLM confidence is itself overconfident (80-100%).
agent_test: Compare checklist verdicts with probability-based confidence ratings.

claim: Argument quality is perspective-dependent: expert, crowd and novice groups differ and models trained on one group do not transfer; only 24 of 103 datasets keep non-aggregated labels.
agent_test: Fix the rater perspective in the judge prompt (audience-relative acceptability).

claim: No study found that gives an LLM the ARS checklist as a verification step and measures end-task answer quality or accuracy at equal tokens. Nearest evidence: a Toulmin critical-question gate (CQoT) gave about +5% judge score on MT-Bench reasoning and math, and a task-specific YES/NO checklist (STICK) beat free-form self-critique on end-task quality; neither used ARS or matched tokens.
agent_test: Main experiment: ARS-checklist Verify vs generic Verify on open answers at equal tokens.

claim: A generic 'review your answer' pass without outside feedback does not improve reasoning accuracy and often lowers it (GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after self-correction; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0 after 5 calls). Any ARS Verify step must beat this baseline, not just no-verify.
agent_test: Include a generic-check arm and a self-consistency arm at equal calls in the ARS experiment.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-10 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: A concrete, answer-specific YES/NO checklist as self-critique improved end-task scores where free-form self-critique hurt (LiveBench reasoning +7.8 points for Command-R+, GPT-4o +0.8, vanilla Self-Refine fell by up to 25 points in some categories); the checklist also raised judge-human exact agreement 46.4% to 52.2%. Instruction-following, not ARS.
agent_test: Write ARS items as concrete yes/no questions about the specific answer, not as abstract advice.

claim: A Toulmin-based critical-question gate on the model's own reasoning plan raised judge scores by about 4.6% (reasoning) and 5.4% (math) over baseline and CoT on MT-Bench for five models, best in 18 of 20 comparisons; the smallest model tested did worse than CoT on reasoning. Tokens were not matched and the judge was GPT-4o.
agent_test: Replicate with equal tokens, ground-truth accuracy and an ARS question set.

claim: LLMs write weak Walton-style critical questions zero-shot: no model of 11 exceeded 57% useful on average, and direct LLM labelling of question usefulness agreed with humans below 0.1. A fixed question list is the safer design.
agent_test: Use fixed ARS questions in the Verify prompt; do not ask the model to invent its own critical questions.

claim: A separately run, targeted verification question set with the draft hidden outperforms a joint check and CoT on factual precision (FACTSCORE 55.9 baseline, 60.8 joint, 63.7 factored, 71.4 factor-and-revise; Llama 2 CoT 41.1 vs zero-shot 41.3). Supports probing sufficiency separately; not tested on argument quality.
agent_test: Run a standalone sufficiency probe with the draft hidden; compare with the full ARS triad at equal cost.

claim: Chain-of-thought gives large gains only on math, symbolic and logical tasks (14.2, 12.3 and 6.9 points) and about 0.7 points elsewhere; on psychology-style judgment tasks CoT lowered accuracy for frontier models (GPT-4o 87.5 to 64.4 on artificial grammar; o1-preview 36.3 points below GPT-4o on a subset). Not tested on ARS judging.
agent_test: A/B the ARS judge: verdict first then rationale vs rationale first, on a human-labelled sufficiency set.

claim: LLM judges favour their own outputs and are swayed by position, sentiment, bandwagon and authority cues (CALM robustness: sentiment .65-.80, bandwagon .61-.79; most models rate own outputs higher even anonymised; GPT-4 pairwise preference flips on swapped order in 25% of cases, GPT-3.5 58%, Llama 89%). Frontier judges mostly resist fallacy-oversight (.92-.99). Hedging bias was not tested.
agent_test: Judge with a different model family than the generator; swap option order; use paired rewrites to test hedge sensitivity.

claim: One irrelevant sentence cuts math accuracy sharply (fewer than 30% of base problems solved across all distractor variants); self-consistency over 20 samples recovers 11+ points micro accuracy and the ignore-irrelevant instruction helps, but the best macro accuracy is only 45%. Relevance filtering of retrieved context needs sampling, not only an instruction.
agent_test: When the agent reads retrieved text, mark and drop irrelevant passages before use and use 3-5 samples for the check.

claim: A model can flag its own unsupported factual claims without retrieval by checking each sentence against resampled answers (SelfCheckGPT prompt variant AUC-PR 93.42 for non-factual vs 72.96 random, 20 samples), but it detects inconsistency, not consistent error.
agent_test: For closed-book answers, test acceptability of factual premises by 3-5 resamples; low agreement means weak support.

claim: Johnson and Blair's account (via SEP) makes acceptability audience-relative, leaves relevance and sufficiency as intuitive graded notions with no numerical measure, and counts a fallacy only as a violation common enough to matter; conductive arguments reach sufficiency cumulatively. A checklist prompt must name the audience and avoid binary verdicts. Books themselves still unread.
agent_test: Add 'for which audience' to acceptability and ask for a degree (weak/moderate/strong), not pass/fail.

claim: Search found no direct study of CASA-style counterfactual objections on frontier models or full answers, no frontier-model sufficiency judge scored on hard items, and no checklist-vs-probability comparison for LLMs. Absence limited by search budget.
agent_test: Treat as open; schedule own experiments.
